Zinc Concepts

Philosophy

Zinc aims for a narrow sweet spot: Express-style routing ergonomics on top of the standard library, without hiding net/http. The framework gives you a small request context and fast routing, but the core contract stays familiar to Go programs.

  • Your app is an http.Handler
  • Startup and shutdown are explicit
  • Routes and middleware share one handler shape
  • Optional behavior is interface-driven through Config
  • Framework conveniences should compose with stdlib handlers and servers

Handler Model

Middleware and routes both use the same type: 

type HandlerFunc func(*Context) error

That keeps the execution model simple. Middleware either returns c.Next() to continue the chain or returns without calling it to stop execution early. 

func auth(c *zinc.Context) error {
    if c.GetHeader("Authorization") == "" {
        return zinc.NewError(zinc.StatusUnauthorized).WithMessage("missing authorization")
    }
    return c.Next()
}

Router Internals

Zinc uses per-method radix trees plus a small route cache for repeated dynamic matches. Static paths resolve quickly, while path params and wildcards are normalized once at registration time and reused during lookup.

  • Routes are stored per HTTP method
  • Path params follow the :name syntax
  • Catch-all params use * and must be final
  • Matched route metadata is stored on the context for the handler
  • Dynamic route cache size is configurable with RouteCacheSize

Route Metadata

Every matched route exposes a stable RouteInfo value: 

type RouteInfo struct {
    Method  string
    Path    string
    Handler string
}

Inside a handler, c.FullPath() returns the registered route pattern, while c.Route() returns the full metadata payload.

Request State And Body Caching

The context caches the request body the first time it is read. That allows helpers like BodyBytes(), BodyString(), and the binder to cooperate on the same request body without forcing the caller to rewind it manually.

Zinc also provides a small request-scoped store through Set, Get, and MustGet. It is intended for middleware-to-handler coordination, not as a service container.

Proxy Trust And Client IP

Zinc only trusts forwarded headers when the direct peer matches TrustedProxies. Without an explicit trust list, helpers like IP() and Scheme() fall back to the direct connection.

  • RemoteIP() is always the socket peer
  • IP() is the first trusted client IP
  • IPs() returns the full forwarded chain when the proxy is trusted
  • Scheme() respects TLS first, then trusted forwarded proto headers

Response Semantics

Zinc guards against accidental double-writes. Once a response helper such as String, JSON, or Redirect writes a response, later writes return ErrResponseAlreadySent.

  • HEAD requests suppress bodies automatically
  • NoContent() defaults to 204 when no explicit status is set
  • Mounted stdlib handlers and file responses mark the context as written immediately
  • The default error handler only writes when nothing has already been sent

Mounting And Stdlib Interop

Zinc is designed to interoperate cleanly with existing net/http code. You can hand Zinc to an http.Server, mount handler trees beneath a prefix, or wrap a single stdlib handler into a Zinc route.

  • app.Handler() returns an http.Handler
  • Mount() strips the mount prefix before forwarding to the mounted handler
  • Wrap() and WrapFunc() adapt stdlib handlers without rewriting them
  • Static/file helpers delegate to standard library file serving behavior

Extension Points

Zinc keeps customization concentrated in a few interfaces on Config: 

type Config struct {
    Binder       Binder
    Validator    Validator
    Renderer     Renderer
    JSONCodec    JSONCodec
    ErrorHandler ErrorHandler
    // ... routing, timeout, proxy, and cache settings
}

That means Zinc handles HTTP mechanics while your application decides how validation, rendering, or JSON encoding should behave.

Performance Notes

The implementation favors small, repeatable optimizations over a custom transport stack:

  • Contexts are reused through a sync.Pool
  • Route params use fixed-size arrays for the common case
  • Dynamic matches can be cached
  • Body reads are cached once per request
  • Static/file responses reuse stdlib serving behavior instead of reimplementing it
